items.title: Start Here
items.text:
1. Follow the Quick Start for your agent.
  2. Read Project Architecture to understand the three-layer model.
  3. Browse the Skill Catalog.
  4. Read How to Use These Skills for discovery paths and adapter behavior.
  5. Read Reviewing and Promoting Skills before publishing reusable lessons.

One source of truth

Portable skill content lives under skills/. Tool-specific connection files live under adapters/. Private agent state stays outside the public repository.

items.title: Do I need all three supported agents?
items.text: No. Install or connect only the path you use. Claude Code and Codex can share the same portable skills, while Hermes reads the canonical directory directly.

items.title: Why are skills and adapters separate?
items.text:
They have different responsibilities:

  • skills/ contains portable workflow knowledge shared by every supported agent.
  • adapters/ contains configuration specific to Claude Code, Codex, or Hermes, plus the runtime-neutral global templates under adapters/shared/.

Keeping those layers separate prevents three copies of the same skill from drifting apart.

items.title: Should this repository contain .claude/skills and .codex/skills?
items.text:
No. Claude Code uses .claude/skills for project-local discovery, but that is a consumer location rather than this repository's canonical store. Codex uses .agents/skills for project-local discovery; .codex/skills is not its documented project skill path.

Installers can place skills into each agent's supported discovery location without duplicating their source in Git.

items.title: Can Hermes use the new layout directly?
items.text:
Yes. Point skills.external_dirs at the nested canonical directory:

skills:
  external_dirs:
    - /absolute/path/to/skills/skills

Start a new session after changing the path.

items.title: Can Hermes edit an external skill directory?
items.text:
Yes, if the process has filesystem write access. External directories are discovery sources, not read-only boundaries. Make shared changes in a separate Git branch or worktree and submit them through review.

A same-named local Hermes skill can take precedence over the shared version.

items.title: What does bootstrap do?
items.text:
./scripts/bootstrap.sh installs the shared and selected provider adapter files into $HOME/.claude and/or $HOME/.codex (or environment overrides). It uses staged writes, timestamped backups, and managed-block merges, and rolls back adapter-file and Git configuration changes on failure. --dry-run performs no filesystem, symlink, or Git configuration changes. --install-skills runs npx skills add before that transaction starts, so a later failure does not uninstall skills it already added.

./scripts/install-codex-agents.sh /path/to/project remains the separate project-level helper; it copies adapters/codex/AGENTS.md into the target project as AGENTS.md.

The installer backs up changed files, refuses a foreign global core.hooksPath, and preserves managed blocks written by other tools, such as <!-- OMC:START -->…<!-- OMC:END -->.

items.title: What is the overlay structure?
items.text:
Use provider-relative paths matching the public adapter tree:

overlay/
├── shared/AGENTS.base.md
├── shared/hooks/...
├── claude/settings.template.json
├── claude/CLAUDE.block.md
└── codex/config.template.toml, hooks.json, agents/...

Only files that exist in the overlay replace their public counterparts before merging. The overlay itself is never copied into this checkout.

items.title: Does this repository publish global configuration?
items.text:
It publishes genericized templates, not anyone's configuration. A runtime-neutral instruction base and lifecycle hook scripts live in adapters/shared/; per-runtime settings templates, hook wiring, subagent definitions, and an injectable CLAUDE.md block live in adapters/claude/ and adapters/codex/.

Real personal content—employer conventions, project trust lists, credentialed MCP servers, private skills, machine paths, session or transcript state—remains forbidden here and belongs in a private overlay repository merged at install time. ADR-0001 records why the earlier "no global configuration" boundary was superseded and what stays out.

items.title: Where should Claude Code sub-agents live?
items.text: At runtime they live in your own ~/.claude/agents/, or with the project that owns them. This repository may publish subagent definition templates under adapters/claude/, but only genericized ones: capability-based roles with no employer context, no private tool names, and no pinned personal model versions. A persona tied to one employer, project, or model choice stays in your private overlay.

items.title: How do I migrate from the old root-level layout?
items.text:
Hermes recursively discovers nested skills, so an existing repository-root entry remains compatible. Point skills.external_dirs at <checkout>/skills if you want discovery limited to the canonical directory. The Codex installer command stays the same. Reinstall or update skills managed by the skills CLI so recorded source paths follow the new layout.

The old layout's global Claude configuration bundle—one user's real ~/.claude tree—was removed and is not coming back. Its replacement is the genericized template layer under adapters/, which shares none of that content; see ADR-0001.

items.title: Can a target project have its own rules?
items.text: Yes. Keep stack- and domain-specific rules in the target project, such as AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or project-local skills. This repository should remain portable and generic.

items.title: bootstrap.sh refuses to merge config.toml with "unrecognized keys" error
items.text:
The Codex bootstrap installer (./scripts/bootstrap.sh --provider codex) now compares the keys in each existing section of your config.toml against the template's declared keys for that section. If it finds keys the template doesn't know about (legacy fields like max_threads from older Codex versions, hand-edited configs, or previously-deprecated names), it refuses to merge and shows:

bootstrap: section [agents] contains unrecognized keys: max_threads. Use --merge-unknown-keys to proceed anyway.

Why? Codex's [agents] table uses serde(flatten) for subtables like [agents.explorer]. When a flattened struct's table also contains keys outside its known field set, serde misreports a valid single-occurrence field as a "duplicate field" error instead of "unknown field". The TOML text is valid, but Codex fails to start.

Fix options:

  1. Manual (recommended): For each legacy key, copy its value to the corresponding new template key before removing the legacy key, then run bootstrap. For example:
  2. max_threads → copy value to max_concurrent_threads_per_session
  3. Then remove the max_threads line

  4. Run bootstrap again

  5. Force merge: Run ./scripts/bootstrap.sh --provider codex --merge-unknown-keys to allow the merge despite unknown keys. The legacy keys will be preserved alongside the new ones (but may cause the false "duplicate field" error in Codex).

items.title: ci-kit onboarding
items.text: This repository is managed by quokkify/ci-kit at v4.3.5. This file is toolkit-owned: ci-kit update rewrites it, so keep project notes elsewhere.

items.title: Modules
items.text:
ci-kit is installed as a set of modules. Every module has its own Copier answers file, .copier-answers.<module>.yml, and a declaration, .ci/modules/<module>.yml. A module owns the files it renders: they are replaced on every update, so change them in ci-kit, not here. Starter files (README.md, .github/pull_request_template.md, and the starters of other modules) are written once and then belong to the project.

core is always installed. It owns the Validate workflow, the template update workflow .github/workflows/copier-update.yml, the PR contract check .github/workflows/pr-contract.yml, and this guide. The other modules, the files each one renders, and their questions are listed in docs/modules.md.

items.title: Pull request titles and release notes
items.text:
Release notes are built from merged pull requests: their title, their labels and three body sections. Nothing else in a PR is published.

  • The type decides who sees the change. feat, fix, perf and revert are listed for users; every other type (deps, chore, ci, test, build, docs, style, refactor) goes under a collapsed "Internal changes" list. The label release-notes: internal moves a feat or fix that only maintainers notice there too.
  • The title is the headline: type(scope): summary, at most 72 characters. Describe what the user notices, not the files or functions you changed.
  • ## Release note is one paragraph of at most 300 characters for someone who only reads release notes: what they can do now, or what was broken and how it showed, plus the input, flag or step to use. It is required for feat, perf and breaking PRs and encouraged for fix. When the title already says everything, add the label release-notes: title-only.
  • ## Usage example (optional, feat) is one short fenced snippet users can copy.
  • A breaking change (! in the title) needs ## Migration with the numbered steps users must take. It is shown first, in a warning box, and is not repeated elsewhere.
  • Everything else in the body (## Description, test plans, tables) is for reviewers.
  • To change a published note, edit the merged PR's title, body or labels; the open release PR is regenerated on the next push to the default branch. Do not edit the release PR body.

The PR contract check reads only the PR event: it re-runs when the title, body or labels change, skips PRs opened by bots (GitHub Apps), and prints the exact section to add. It reports problems as warnings until the toolkit switches it to enforce.

items.title: Check the installation
items.text:
pip install "git+https://github.com/quokkify/ci-kit@v4.3.5"
ci-kit doctor --repo .

ci-kit doctor reports missing or conflicting answers files, invalid module declarations, and files that differ from the template render. Each finding names an error code with a runbook in docs/errors/.

items.title: Update to a newer toolkit release
items.text:
Run the Update project template workflow; it updates every module to the latest release and pushes a branch for review. To update by hand:

git switch main && git pull --ff-only
export TOOLKIT_REF="$(gh release view --repo quokkify/ci-kit --json tagName --jq .tagName)"
git switch -c "chore/update-ci-kit-${TOOLKIT_REF}"
pip install "git+https://github.com/quokkify/ci-kit@${TOOLKIT_REF}"
ci-kit update --repo . --to "$TOOLKIT_REF"
git push -u origin HEAD
gh pr create --fill

ci-kit update commits one update per module and stops on the first Copier conflict.

items.title: Add a module
items.text:
copier copy --trust --vcs-ref v4.3.5 -a .copier-answers.<module>.yml -d module=<module> gh:quokkify/ci-kit .

Change a module's answers by re-running copier update -a .copier-answers.<module>.yml --data <question>=<value>. Question names and allowed values are defined in copier.yml.

items.title: Project Architecture
items.text: The project treats agent portability as three connected problems: reusable knowledge, recoverable private state, and safe execution.

items.title: Skills Hub
items.text:
Public and portable. The canonical skills/ tree stores reviewed workflows once, while adapters connect provider-specific discovery mechanisms and supply genericized global templates.

  • versioned skill packages;
  • references, templates, and helpers;
  • runtime-neutral global instruction base and lifecycle hooks in adapters/shared/;
  • per-runtime wiring templates in adapters/claude/ and adapters/codex/;
  • privacy-aware promotion through pull requests;
  • validation and release gates.

items.title: Configuration Vault
items.text:
Private and recoverable. A separate vault preserves the real configuration overlay and a restore manifest without weakening the public boundary.

  • employer conventions, project trust lists, credentialed MCP servers, private skills;
  • machine-specific Hermes, Claude Code, and Codex configuration;
  • the overlay merged over the public templates at install time;
  • backup and restore tooling;
  • repository URL, exact revision, and dirty-state manifest;
  • encrypted or access-controlled secret storage.

items.title: Agent Harness
items.text:
Bounded and observable. The harness turns skills into safe runtime behavior by controlling the tools and feedback exposed to an agent.

  • typed operations and fail-closed validation;
  • least-privilege permissions and approval gates;
  • deterministic observations and durable handles;
  • cancellation, retries, recovery, and audit evidence.

items.title: Trust Boundaries
items.text:
The three layers cooperate, but they do not share the same publication or security policy.

Data Public Skills Hub Private Vault Runtime Harness Portable workflows and generic references Yes Optional manifest reference Read-only consumption Provider connection instructions Sanitized examples only Full private configuration Loaded at runtime Global instruction base, hook scripts, settings and subagent definitions Genericized templates only Real overlay values Merged result loaded at runtime Employer identifiers, project trust lists, machine paths, pinned personal model choices Never Owned here Applied at runtime Credentials and private keys Never Encrypted/access-controlled Injected without model-visible logging Memories, chats, sessions, runtime databases Never Backup only when explicitly selected Scoped runtime access Tool schemas and safety contracts Yes Not required Enforced

The vault is not a directory inside this repository

A public clone, Git history, release artifact, or documentation build must never contain raw agent-home snapshots, credentials, memories, transcripts, or private runtime state.

Publishing a global adapter template does not relax this. A template is derived from a real setup by removing everything specific to it; it is never a copy of one. scripts/validate_repo.py mechanically rejects machine home paths, local secret-store paths, forbidden state filenames, private state directories, and symlinks, but a passing validator is not a substitute for reading the diff.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Learn from completed work] --> B[Review and sanitize]
    B --> C[Publish portable skill]
    C --> D[Load through provider adapter]
    V[Restore private configuration] --> D
    D --> E[Execute through harness]
    E --> F[Observe and verify]
    F --> A

    subgraph Public[Public repository]
      B
      C
    end

    subgraph Private[Private boundary]
      V
    end

    subgraph Runtime[Runtime boundary]
      D
      E
      F
    end

This creates a controlled feedback loop:

  1. Learn from real work.
  2. Sanitize and review the reusable lesson.
  3. Publish it once in the hub.
  4. Preserve private provider state separately.
  5. Execute safely through a bounded harness.
  6. Verify results before the next lesson is promoted.

items.title: Current Repository Scope
items.text:
This repository implements the public skills hub, provider adapters including genericized global templates, validation/synchronization tooling, and reusable harness-design guidance. The private overlay and configuration vault is an architectural companion, not a public package shipped here. scripts/bootstrap.sh installs the templates with staged writes, timestamped backups, and managed-block merges.

Use these entry points:

  • Quick Start — connect Claude Code, Codex, or Hermes.
  • Decision Records — why the global-adapter boundary moved.
  • Skill Catalog — browse the portable workflows.
  • How to Use These Skills — understand provider discovery and adapter behavior.
  • agent-harness-design — design safe tool and observation contracts.
  • agent-knowledge-lifecycle — maintain the public/private knowledge boundary.

items.title: Quick Start
items.text:
Clone the repository and run commands from its root:

git clone https://github.com/quokkify/skills.git
cd skills

items.title: Required companions
items.text: Claude Code requires oh-my-claudecode and superpowers; Codex requires superpowers. Hermes requires neither and must not load superpowers. The installer warns when one is missing, and a SessionStart hook tells the agent to report it before working. See ADR-0003.

items.title: Claude Code
items.text:
Install the portable skills and Claude adapter:

./scripts/bootstrap.sh --provider claude --install-skills

The installer merges genericized templates into the selected runtime home, backs up changed files with a timestamp, and preserves foreign managed blocks. Add --overlay /path/to/private-overlay to layer private files after the public base. The overlay is read in place and is never copied into the checkout.

Your own employer conventions, project trust lists, credentialed MCP servers, private skills, and machine paths stay in your private overlay, outside this repository. See ADR-0001.

items.title: Codex
items.text:
Install the portable skills and Codex adapter:

./scripts/bootstrap.sh --provider codex --install-skills

The global Codex instruction file is a symlink to the checkout's shared base. After installation, open the Codex TUI and run /hooks to approve command hooks. For project-specific instructions, copy adapters/codex/AGENTS.md into a target project:

./scripts/install-codex-agents.sh /path/to/your/project

Codex discovers project-local skills from .agents/skills, not .codex/skills.

For a manual installation of the full Codex adapter (including hooks, configuration, and agent definitions):

  1. Set $CODEX_HOME (defaults to $HOME/.codex). Export it so it stays set across each of the following commands, even if you run them as separate shell invocations: 
    export CODEX_HOME="${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}"
  2. Create necessary directories: 
    mkdir -p "$CODEX_HOME/agents" "$CODEX_HOME/hooks"
  3. Copy shared hook scripts (required for hooks in hooks.json to function), backing up any file already there: 
    for f in sessionstart-repo-context.sh pretooluse-bash-guard.sh completion-gate.sh hook-lib.sh; do
  [ -e "$CODEX_HOME/hooks/$f" ] && cp "$CODEX_HOME/hooks/$f" "$CODEX_HOME/hooks/$f.bak"
  cp "adapters/shared/hooks/$f" "$CODEX_HOME/hooks/"
done
  4. Copy Codex-specific configuration and agent definitions, backing up any file already there: 
    # Base config — do not overwrite an existing config.toml
if [ ! -f "$CODEX_HOME/config.toml" ]; then
  cp adapters/codex/config.template.toml "$CODEX_HOME/config.toml"
else
  echo "Warning: $CODEX_HOME/config.toml exists, skipping copy. Merge manually if needed."
fi
[ -e "$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json" ] && cp "$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json" "$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json.bak"
cp adapters/codex/hooks.json "$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json"
for f in adapters/codex/agents/*.toml; do
  base="$(basename "$f")"
  [ -e "$CODEX_HOME/agents/$base" ] && cp "$CODEX_HOME/agents/$base" "$CODEX_HOME/agents/$base.bak"
  cp "$f" "$CODEX_HOME/agents/"
done
  5. In the Codex TUI, run /hooks and approve the hook entries.

Note: The current hook set includes SessionStart, PreToolUse (bash-guard), and Stop. Other runtime events are not covered by the shipped hook scripts; you may add additional hooks as needed.

items.title: Hermes
items.text:
Add the canonical skill directory—not the repository root—to the Hermes configuration:

skills:
  external_dirs:
    - /absolute/path/to/skills/skills

Start a new Hermes session after changing the discovery path. Keep shared edits on an isolated Git branch or worktree; an external directory is not a write-protection boundary.

items.title: Claude Code and Codex Together
items.text:
./scripts/bootstrap.sh --install-skills

The default provider is all. Use --dry-run to inspect the complete operation list safely.

items.title: Update the Shared Checkout
items.text:
From its clean main branch:

./scripts/sync-shared-skills.sh

The sync helper updates the Git checkout. Rerun the Codex adapter installer when its copied AGENTS.md changes.

items.title: Decision Records
items.text:
Durable architecture decisions for this repository. Each record keeps its context, the alternatives that were genuinely considered, and the consequences — including the negative ones — readable after the discussion that produced it has been forgotten.

The format follows the in-repo architecture-decision-records skill. A decision is never rewritten to pretend it was different; it is superseded by a newer record.

ADR Status Decision ADR-0001 accepted Publish genericized global agent adapters, and keep every user's real configuration in a private overlay ADR-0002 accepted Reference quokkify/project-toolkit by its exact release tag and let the template own release.yml in full ADR-0003 accepted Require oh-my-claudecode on Claude Code and superpowers on Claude Code and Codex, keep Hermes free of superpowers, and drop ECC as a role and rule source ADR-0004 superseded in part by ADR-0005 State one workflow precedence order, give oh-my-claudecode the plan and execute steps on Claude Code and superpowers on Codex, and delete orchestrator-workflow and refactor-workflow ADR-0005 accepted Let the superpowers chain own the process on Claude Code, keep oh-my-claudecode for agents, routing, and hooks, and run its workflows only on explicit request

items.title: ADR-0001: Publish genericized global agent adapters instead of no global configuration
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-13
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Context
items.text:
Until this decision, the repository documented a hard boundary in five places: no global CLAUDE.md, no sub-agent personas, no output styles, no status lines, and no project-specific commands. The FAQ additionally recorded that a former "global Claude configuration bundle" had been deliberately removed.

That boundary was correct for the artifact that existed at the time. The only global configuration available to publish was one user's real agent home: employer conventions, project trust lists, credentialed MCP server entries, employer-only skills, and absolute machine paths. Publishing it would have leaked private context, and it would not have helped anyone else, because almost none of it was portable.

Two things changed:

  1. The content can be genericized and the result can be checked mechanically. scripts/validate_repo.py rejects machine-specific home paths, Windows home paths, local secret-store paths, agent-local and credential-state filenames, private runtime state directories, symlinks, and broken or repository-escaping Markdown links, on every tracked file. That converts "please review carefully" into a gate that fails a pull request.
  2. The runtimes converged. Codex CLI 0.146 gained native hooks, subagents, and skills using the same hook JSON contract as Claude Code. A single runtime-neutral base plus thin per-runtime wiring is now genuinely portable, rather than a Claude-only bundle wearing a cross-runtime label.

Meanwhile the underlying need did not go away: a user who installs the portable skills still has to hand-build the global layer that decides what loads before any skill runs, and there was no reviewed starting point for it anywhere.
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Publish the global agent configuration layer as templates and genericized defaults, and keep every user's real configuration out.

The repository is organized in three layers:

  1. Shared portable skills — skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md. Unchanged, and still the only source of truth for portable workflow knowledge. A skill body is never duplicated into an adapter.
  2. Genericized global adapters — adapters/shared/ holds a runtime-neutral global instruction base plus cross-runtime lifecycle hook scripts and git hooks. adapters/claude/ and adapters/codex/ hold per-runtime templates: settings and config templates, hook wiring, subagent definitions, and an injectable CLAUDE.md block.
  3. Private overlay — the user's real content lives in a separate private repository and is merged over the templates at install time. It is not a directory inside this repository.

A published adapter must be derived from a real setup by removing everything specific to it, never a copy of one.

This supersedes the earlier "no global configuration is published" boundary. It does not restore the removed bundle: none of that content returns, and the removal decision remains correct for what it removed.
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: What remains forbidden
items.text:
• real credentials, tokens, and private endpoints;
  • employer, client, and private-project identifiers, including internal repository, tracker, and CI paths;
  • any person's name or personal identifiers;
  • machine-specific home paths — use $HOME, ~/.claude/..., ~/.codex/..., or /path/to/...;
  • session, transcript, memory, and runtime-database state, and raw agent-home snapshots;
  • pinned personal model versions or one user's routing policy presented as a default;
  • any user's actual private overlay, in whole or in part.
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Alternatives considered
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Keep the boundary and put the whole global layer in a private repository
items.text:
• Benefits: zero leak surface; no new review obligation; nothing to keep in step.
  • Costs and risks: the reusable part of the layer — hook contracts, capability-based subagent shapes, a neutral instruction base — stays invisible, so every consumer rebuilds it and the shared skills keep assuming a global layer that this project never shows.
  • Why it was not selected: it protects content that does not need protecting, at the cost of the layer being unreviewable and unshared.
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Publish the real personal configuration
items.text:
• Benefits: no genericization work; the published artifact is known to function end to end.
  • Costs and risks: leaks employer context, trust lists, and machine paths; is unusable to others without editing; would be rejected by the existing validator and by the repository's SECURITY.md boundary.
  • Why it was not selected: it is the exact failure the original removal was meant to prevent.
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Chosen: genericized templates in public, real overlay in private
items.text:
• Benefits: the portable part is shared and reviewed; the private part keeps its trust boundary; the split is enforced by an existing mechanical gate.
  • Costs and risks: two repositories must stay in step, and every future adapter edit needs a leak review.
  • Why it was selected: it is the only option that makes the layer reusable without moving any private content into a public clone.
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Consequences
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Positive
items.text:
• The global layer becomes a reviewed artifact with a public diff, instead of undocumented local state.
  • Consumers get a working starting point for hooks, settings, and subagent definitions rather than a prohibition.
  • One shared base serves both Claude Code and Codex, so a hook or instruction fix lands once.
  • The public/private line is now written down as a rule an installer and a validator can both apply.
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Negative
items.text:
• Ongoing leak-review burden. Every future adapter edit is a potential disclosure, and unlike a skill body it may carry settings values, tool names, or paths that look innocuous. Mitigation: scripts/validate_repo.py plus Gitleaks on every pull request and the default branch, and the adapter-boundary checklist in shared-skill-library-maintenance. Neither proves a file is appropriate to publish.
  • Two repositories to keep in step. A template change can break an overlay that patched the same file. Mitigation: keep templates minimal and treat the overlay as authoritative on conflict.
  • Overwrite risk at install time. Merging templates into a live agent home can clobber existing configuration. Mitigation: any installer must back up rather than overwrite, and must preserve managed blocks written by other tools, such as <!-- OMC:START -->…<!-- OMC:END -->. No installer ships with this decision; templates are copied manually until one lands.
  • Genericization can hide breakage. A template with the specifics removed may no longer be a configuration that actually works. Mitigation: exercise the templates from a scratch agent home before claiming they install cleanly.
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: Follow-up and review triggers
items.text:
• The follow-up installer (scripts/bootstrap.sh) must implement backup-not-overwrite and foreign-managed-block preservation before it is documented as available.
  • Revisit if the hook or settings contract diverges again between runtimes, which would make one shared base dishonest.
  • Revisit if a leak reaches the public branch, or if template drift makes the overlay unmergeable: either signals that the split is in the wrong place.
  • Supersede this record rather than editing it if the repository later decides to stop publishing the adapter layer.
path: ADR-0001: Publish generic global agent adapters

items.title: ADR-0002: Reference project-toolkit by its release tag instead of a commit digest
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-09-01
path: ADR-0002: Reference project-toolkit by release tag

items.title: Context
items.text:
.github/workflows/release.yml is owned by the quokkify/project-toolkit Copier template. The template renders the reusable release workflow as an exact release tag:

uses: quokkify/project-toolkit/.github/workflows/release-please.yml@v2.19.0

This repository instead held a 40-character commit digest with the tag as a trailing comment, and tests/test_release_configuration.py required that form. The digest never came from the template, and it never came from Renovate either: every digest that line has ever carried was written by hand while reconciling a template update, and no automated commit has ever touched the file. The test encoded a convention that only manual reconciliation had been sustaining.

That reconciliation ended. The shared preset now disables Renovate for the workflow paths the template owns, release.yml among them, so that a project-side pin and a template-side pin cannot fight over the same line — and the template update automation applies the rendered file unattended rather than pausing for a human to re-pin it. Each copier update therefore rewrote the file to the tag form, the test rejected it, and the run ended in a conflict:

[failed] quokkify/skills: Copier produced conflict files: .github/workflows/release.yml.rej

This repository was the last public consumer the fleet automation could not update on the current template; the consumers that call the toolkit's release workflow all reference it by tag and update unattended.

The requirement the test encoded was also stricter than the contract the toolkit itself enforces. The template-owned check in .github/workflows/validate.yml accepts either form:

pinned_release = len(reference) == 40 and all(char in "0123456789abcdef" for char in reference) and comment == answers["toolkit_version"]
if reference != answers["toolkit_version"] and not pinned_release:
    raise SystemExit(f"{path} uses toolkit {reference}, expected {answers['toolkit_version']}")

Divergences travelled with the pin. The file predated the template's release_mode answer, so it carried a hand-written manifest configuration, and it had also drifted in its workflow name, its workflow_dispatch trigger, and its concurrency group.
path: ADR-0002: Reference project-toolkit by release tag

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Reference quokkify/project-toolkit by its exact release tag, and let the template own release.yml in full.

The unit test now applies the toolkit's own contract rather than a narrower one: a reference identifies the toolkit release workflow at the answered toolkit_version when it is either that exact tag or a full 40-character digest whose comment names that tag. Both forms pass, so a future decision to re-pin by hand does not require another test change.

release_mode: manifest is recorded in .copier-answers.yml, so the template renders this repository's manifest configuration instead of the single-version default, and the workflow is aligned with the rendered shape in every other respect. The template update to v2.19.0 is applied in the same change, which consumes the one-time transition conflict; subsequent updates apply cleanly and change nothing but the version.
path: ADR-0002: Reference project-toolkit by release tag

items.title: Alternatives considered
path: ADR-0002: Reference project-toolkit by release tag

items.title: Keep the digest and own the release workflow outright
items.text:
Stop rendering release.yml from the template, and maintain the release workflow under a project-owned filename. q4j is the closest precedent in the organization: it keeps a project-owned release-please.yml and no rendered release.yml, though it goes further than this alternative would by calling googleapis/release-please-action directly rather than the toolkit's reusable workflow.

  • Benefits: keeps the immutable pin; makes the existing divergence honest instead of leaving a template-owned file that automation keeps fighting; upstream fleet automation deliberately leaves digests in project-owned files alone rather than downgrading them to tags.
  • Costs and risks: the release workflow is maintained by hand indefinitely and stops receiving template fixes; it drifts from the other consumers; the repository accepts unbounded maintenance to protect one line.
  • Why it was not selected: the strictness it buys is small next to the trust already extended to the template, and the maintenance it costs does not end.
path: ADR-0002: Reference project-toolkit by release tag

items.title: Keep the digest and re-enable Renovate for release.yml
items.text:
Restore the digest and let Renovate re-pin the rendered tag after each template update, which is the arrangement the file's history had always approximated by hand.

  • Benefits: no test change; the digest survives without manual reconciliation.
  • Costs and risks: creates exactly the double ownership the shared preset was introduced to prevent. Renovate moves the pin, the next copier update lands on the moved pin, and the conflict returns in a file this repository never edited.
  • Why it was not selected: it automates the manual step that produced the problem, rather than removing the divergence.
path: ADR-0002: Reference project-toolkit by release tag

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
This is a real loosening of supply-chain strictness, and it is the cost of the decision rather than an oversight. A tag is mutable: whoever can move v2.19.0 in quokkify/project-toolkit can change what this repository executes at release time, without a commit here. A digest cannot be moved.

What limits that exposure is ownership, not the pin. The toolkit is a first-party repository in the same organization, its release tags are never rewritten by policy, and third-party actions inside it remain digest-pinned. The tag is trusted here in the same way and to the same degree as the template that renders it, which this repository already executes on every push.

In exchange, release.yml stops being a file that automation and this repository take turns rewriting. Template updates land unattended, and the divergence that made every update conflict is gone rather than merely re-resolved.
path: ADR-0002: Reference project-toolkit by release tag

items.title: ADR-0003: Require oh-my-claudecode on Claude Code and superpowers on Claude Code and Codex
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-20
path: ADR-0003: Require oh-my-claudecode and superpowers companions

items.title: Context
items.text:
The adapters assumed one orchestration layer but never named it. orchestrator-workflow deferred to Everything Claude Code (ECC) whenever a target repository used it, and the shared base carried ECC-derived defaults: an 80 percent coverage target, fixed function and file size limits, immutability as a default, and a Java-specific nullability rule. On a machine where oh-my-claudecode supplies the agents, ECC role names such as tdd-guide, doc-updater, and docs-lookup do not resolve, so the guidance pointed at roles that did not exist and competed with the catalog that did.

Superpowers supplies process discipline — brainstorming, test-driven development, systematic debugging, verification before completion — on both Claude Code and Codex CLI. Nothing checked that it was installed, so a missing plugin failed silently: the agent reconstructed the workflows from memory or skipped them.
path: ADR-0003: Require oh-my-claudecode and superpowers companions

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• Claude Code requires oh-my-claudecode. It owns the agent catalog, model routing, and the plan, execute, review, and verify workflows on that runtime.
  • Claude Code and Codex CLI require superpowers. Its skills are the discipline applied inside each orchestration step; when both companions offer a workflow for the same step, oh-my-claudecode drives orchestration and superpowers supplies discipline.
  • A shared SessionStart hook, sessionstart-prerequisites.sh, checks the companions for its runtime and tells the agent to stop and report a missing one before substantive work. scripts/bootstrap.sh prints the same result as non-fatal warnings.
  • Hermes requires no companion and must not load superpowers, neither the plugin nor a curated subset. See the Hermes adapter for the reasons.
  • ECC is no longer a role or rule source. The skills adapted from ECC stay, with attribution, because they are standalone and do not depend on an ECC installation.
path: ADR-0003: Require oh-my-claudecode and superpowers companions

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• Keep ECC as the preferred role catalog. Rejected: two catalogs with overlapping role names produce unresolvable delegations, and ECC's coding-style defaults override project conventions.
  • Require superpowers on Hermes too. Rejected after reviewing Hermes 0.22.2: its bundled software-development-lifecycle skill already covers most of the same process topics, the skill index truncates descriptions to 60 characters so broad Use when… triggers fire on ops and chat turns, a hand-picked subset breaks on cross-skill references to subagent-driven-development, and Hermes can patch skills it loads from external directories, which silently edits a pinned checkout.
  • Fail the installer when a companion is missing. Rejected: companions are installed through each runtime's own plugin flow, which may happen after the hub is installed. The session hook enforces the requirement where the agent actually works.
  • State the requirement in prose only. Rejected: the requirement is mechanically checkable, and the repository's rule is that checkable rules become hooks.
path: ADR-0003: Require oh-my-claudecode and superpowers companions

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The public adapters are now opinionated about two third-party companions. A reader who does not use them must opt out with SKILLS_HUB_SKIP_HOOKS=prerequisites and override the instruction in a private overlay.
  • Detection relies on installation markers — the oh-my-claudecode CLAUDE.md block, enabled plugin entries, the omc CLI, a superpowers skill directory. A companion installed some other way reads as missing until the hook learns that marker.
  • Removing the ECC-derived defaults means coverage targets and size limits now come from each project rather than the global base.
path: ADR-0003: Require oh-my-claudecode and superpowers companions

items.title: ADR-0004: Set one workflow precedence order and give each runtime a single plan-and-execute owner
items.text:
• Status: superseded in part by ADR-0005 (Claude Code process owner and precedence order)
  • Date: 2026-10-20
path: ADR-0004: Workflow precedence between companions and the shared base

items.title: Context
items.text:
ADR-0003 made oh-my-claudecode required on Claude Code and superpowers required on Claude Code and Codex CLI. A review afterwards found that the instructions now conflict in three places.

  • The shared base says to ask at most one round of clarifying questions and to go straight to the change for small work. Superpowers brainstorming asks one question at a time and waits for approval before any design is implemented. Both claim to govern the same turn.
  • On Claude Code, oh-my-claudecode and superpowers each ship a full plan-and-execute chain (plan/ralplan/execute against writing-plans/executing-plans/subagent-driven-development), and orchestrator-workflow claimed a third "top-level phase structure" that it said MUST be followed exactly. The adapter's only tie-breaker was one sentence saying oh-my-claudecode drives orchestration and superpowers supplies discipline.
  • The Codex adapter and the orchestrator-workflow role catalog listed role names — planner, backend-developer, code-researcher, implementation-generalist, and others — that no shipped configuration defines, so delegations to them could not resolve. refactor-workflow duplicated the five-phase orchestration with a refactor slant and added fixed style rules that override project conventions.
path: ADR-0004: Workflow precedence between companions and the shared base

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The Claude Code bullets and the precedence order below are superseded by ADR-0005: on Claude Code the superpowers chain owns the process and oh-my-claudecode supplies agents, routing, and hooks.

  • The shared base states one precedence order: user and project instructions, then the runtime's orchestration companion workflow (oh-my-claudecode on Claude Code), then superpowers process discipline, then the base defaults.
  • The base's interaction and ceremony-sizing defaults apply only when no required companion process skill applies. When superpowers brainstorming applies to new feature or design work, its one-question-at-a-time approval flow governs.
  • On Claude Code, oh-my-claudecode owns planning and execution. Superpowers contributes brainstorming for design exploration and the discipline skills — test-driven-development, systematic-debugging, verification-before-completion, receiving-code-review. Its writing-plans, executing-plans, and subagent-driven-development are not used there, and neither is orchestrator-workflow.
  • On Codex, the superpowers chain owns planning and execution, and superpowers also supplies the dispatch mechanics through using-superpowers/references/codex-tools.md and subagent-driven-development. The Codex adapter keeps only roles, hooks, and cost policy, and its budget modes map onto superpowers' own: executing-plans inline for cheap, subagent-driven-development for thorough, never a mode without review. orchestrator-workflow is deleted.
  • Role catalogs list only roles that exist: the Codex built-ins default, worker, and explorer, the shipped explorer, reviewer, and docs_researcher, and project-local roles from the target repository's .codex/agents, which take precedence.
  • refactor-workflow is deleted. Its useful core — targeted versus exploratory refactors, behavior preservation, tests green before and after — moves into a Refactoring section of the shared base, so it also serves runtimes without a companion. Its style rules and its mandatory plan-approval gate are dropped.
path: ADR-0004: Workflow precedence between companions and the shared base

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• Let superpowers own planning on Claude Code as well. Rejected: oh-my-claudecode's plan and execute workflows are wired to its own agent catalog and model routing, so running superpowers' chain on top would route delegation around the companion that owns it.
  • Keep orchestrator-workflow as the top-level phase structure on every runtime. Rejected: a third phase model on top of two companion chains is exactly the conflict this record resolves, and it adds ceremony without adding a capability either companion lacks.
  • Keep orchestrator-workflow as a Codex delegation backend guide. Rejected: superpowers' Codex tool mapping covers dispatch, briefs, waiting, model selection, and review more precisely, and the rest duplicated the Codex adapter.
  • Keep refactor-workflow as a separate skill. Rejected: it repeated the orchestration phases nearly verbatim, and its only distinct content fits in one short section.
  • Keep the invented role names as illustrative examples. Rejected: agents read role lists as instructions, and a name that does not resolve produces a failed delegation rather than a hint.
path: ADR-0004: Workflow precedence between companions and the shared base

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Each runtime has exactly one owner for planning and execution, and the precedence order resolves the remaining overlaps without per-skill tie-breakers.
  • The base's "at most one round of questions" default no longer applies to feature design work on runtimes with superpowers, so those sessions ask more questions before implementation.
  • Users of other harnesses lose the bundled fallback role names. They must define roles in the target repository or delegate to whatever the harness exposes.
  • Anyone who invoked refactor-workflow or orchestrator-workflow directly must switch to the Refactoring section of the shared base and the runtime's companion: superpowers on Claude Code (since ADR-0005) and on Codex.
  • Harnesses with neither companion lose the bundled orchestration guide and rely on the shared base's delegation rules.
path: ADR-0004: Workflow precedence between companions and the shared base

items.title: ADR-0005: Let the superpowers chain own the process on Claude Code and keep oh-my-claudecode for agents
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-21
  • Supersedes: the Claude Code decision and the precedence order in ADR-0004
path: ADR-0005: superpowers owns the process on Claude Code

items.title: Context
items.text:
ADR-0004 gave oh-my-claudecode the plan and execute steps on Claude Code and kept only brainstorming and the discipline skills from superpowers. In use, that split cuts the superpowers chain at its first handoff:

  • brainstorming ends by invoking writing-plans; that is its only terminal state on the architectural path. The adapter forbade the very next step the skill requires, so every design session hit a conflict between the skill and the adapter and resolved it ad hoc, sometimes one way and sometimes the other.
  • ADR-0004 rejected superpowers on Claude Code because oh-my-claudecode's plan and execute workflows are wired to its agent catalog and model routing. subagent-driven-development carries its whole task in prompt templates and requires only that each dispatch names a model. Its templates name general-purpose as the subagent type, but nothing in the flow depends on that type, so the adapter can route the same templates to oh-my-claudecode agents without bypassing the companion.
  • Codex already runs the superpowers chain. Two process owners in one hub means two process descriptions to keep consistent.
path: ADR-0005: superpowers owns the process on Claude Code

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• On Claude Code, the superpowers chain owns the process: brainstorming → writing-plans → the execution mode the user picks at its handoff, subagent-driven-development or executing-plans. Each execution mode runs its own reviews and ends in finishing-a-development-branch. The discipline skills — test-driven-development, systematic-debugging, requesting-code-review, receiving-code-review, verification-before-completion — apply wherever they fit.
  • oh-my-claudecode stays required and owns the agent catalog, model routing, and hooks. The adapter overrides the templates' general-purpose subagent type: implementers and fixes go to executor, reviewers to code-reviewer. The skill's prompt template replaces the agent's default task and report format, and the skill's model tiers map to haiku, sonnet, and opus.
  • oh-my-claudecode workflows (plan, ralplan, deep-interview, execute, review, verify, autopilot, ralph, team, ultragoal) run only when the user types the slash command or asks for one by name; a keyword detected in incidental text does not count. The adapter states that the workflow list in oh-my-claudecode's managed block does not set the process.
  • The shared precedence order becomes: user and project instructions, then the superpowers process chain, then the runtime's orchestration layer, then the base defaults. A marker-delimited block that a companion's tooling writes into the user's instruction file ranks as that companion, not as a user instruction.
  • The rest of ADR-0004 stands: interaction defaults yield to companion process skills, Codex is unchanged, and orchestrator-workflow and refactor-workflow stay deleted.
path: ADR-0005: superpowers owns the process on Claude Code

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• Keep oh-my-claudecode as the process owner and allow writing-plans as an exception. Rejected: the chain continues past planning into an execution mode and finishing-a-development-branch, so a single exception moves the conflict one step later instead of removing it.
  • Drop oh-my-claudecode on Claude Code. Rejected: superpowers ships no agent catalog, model routing, or hooks, and the user-invoked autonomous modes have no superpowers equivalent.
  • Let both chains coexist and choose per task. Rejected: this is the overlap ADR-0004 removed; an agent choosing between two process owners on every turn is the failure being fixed.
path: ADR-0005: superpowers owns the process on Claude Code

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Claude Code and Codex run the same superpowers chain; the adapters differ in dispatch mechanics and agent catalogs.
  • Specs land in docs/superpowers/specs/ and plans in docs/superpowers/plans/ and are committed to the target repository, unlike oh-my-claudecode's git-ignored .omc/plans/.
  • oh-my-claudecode reviewer agents carry their own output contracts and cannot write files. Dispatches rely on the superpowers template overriding the contract, and fixes always go to executor.
  • The oh-my-claudecode managed block still lists its own canonical workflows. Agents must apply the precedence rule for managed blocks to ignore it.
  • Users who relied on plan or ralplan running by default must now invoke them by name.
path: ADR-0005: superpowers owns the process on Claude Code

items.title: How to Use These Skills
items.text:
This repository has three intentionally separate layers:

  1. skills/ — portable workflow knowledge and the only source of truth.
  2. adapters/ — optional integration files and genericized global templates for a specific agent runtime, plus the runtime-neutral base under adapters/shared/.
  3. A private overlay, kept in a separate repository, holding your real personal, employer, and machine-specific configuration.

Layers 1 and 2 are public because they contain no one's actual configuration. Layer 3 is never published here.

items.title: Claude Code
items.text:
Install the portable skills with the skills CLI. Claude Code supports personal skills under ~/.claude/skills and project skills under .claude/skills.

Global configuration is separate and optional. The templates under adapters/shared/ and adapters/claude/ are genericized: a runtime-neutral instruction base, lifecycle hook scripts, settings and hook wiring, subagent definitions, and an injectable CLAUDE.md block. They contain no employer identifiers, credentials, machine paths, or pinned personal model versions. Install them with scripts/bootstrap.sh, which merges an optional private overlay over the templates and backs up rather than overwrites existing files, or copy them manually.

items.title: Codex
items.text:
Install the same portable skills for Codex. Codex discovers repository skills by walking from the current directory to the repository root and looking under .agents/skills; personal skills live under $HOME/.agents/skills.

The optional ./scripts/install-codex-agents.sh /path/to/project helper copies adapters/codex/AGENTS.md into a target project. The repository deliberately does not maintain a duplicate .codex/skills tree.

For a manual installation of the full Codex adapter (including hooks, configuration, and agent definitions):

  1. Set $CODEX_HOME (defaults to $HOME/.codex). Export it so it stays set across each of the following commands, even if you run them as separate shell invocations: 
    export CODEX_HOME="${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}"
  2. Create necessary directories: 
    mkdir -p "$CODEX_HOME/agents" "$CODEX_HOME/hooks"
  3. Copy shared hook scripts (required for hooks in hooks.json to function), backing up any file already there: 
    for f in sessionstart-repo-context.sh sessionstart-prerequisites.sh pretooluse-bash-guard.sh completion-gate.sh hook-lib.sh; do
  [ -e "$CODEX_HOME/hooks/$f" ] && cp "$CODEX_HOME/hooks/$f" "$CODEX_HOME/hooks/$f.bak"
  cp "adapters/shared/hooks/$f" "$CODEX_HOME/hooks/"
done
  4. Copy Codex-specific configuration and agent definitions, backing up any file already there: 
    # Base config — do not overwrite an existing config.toml
if [ ! -f "$CODEX_HOME/config.toml" ]; then
  cp adapters/codex/config.template.toml "$CODEX_HOME/config.toml"
else
  echo "Warning: $CODEX_HOME/config.toml exists, skipping copy. Merge manually if needed."
fi
[ -e "$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json" ] && cp "$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json" "$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json.bak"
cp adapters/codex/hooks.json "$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json"
for f in adapters/codex/agents/*.toml; do
  base="$(basename "$f")"
  [ -e "$CODEX_HOME/agents/$base" ] && cp "$CODEX_HOME/agents/$base" "$CODEX_HOME/agents/$base.bak"
  cp "$f" "$CODEX_HOME/agents/"
done
  5. In the Codex TUI, run /hooks and approve the hook entries.

Note: The current hook set includes SessionStart, PreToolUse (bash-guard), and Stop. Other runtime events are not covered by the shipped hook scripts; you may add additional hooks as needed.

items.title: Hermes
items.text:
Hermes reads the canonical directory directly:

skills:
  external_dirs:
    - /absolute/path/to/skills/skills

Start a new session after changing the path or updating the checkout. External directories remain writable when filesystem permissions allow it, so use a Git branch or worktree for shared changes rather than editing the stable checkout through skill-management tools.

A same-named local Hermes skill can take precedence over an external one. Resolve collisions before assuming the shared copy is active.

items.title: Safe Checkout Updates
items.text:
From a clean direct checkout on main:

./scripts/sync-shared-skills.sh

The helper validates one exact fetched commit with a preserved copy of the current validator, rejects ahead or diverged history, disables Git hooks during the fast-forward, and never executes fetched scripts. Concurrent branch or worktree changes cause an error rather than a false success report.

The helper updates the repository only. If you copied the Codex adapter into another location, rerun its installer when adapters/codex/AGENTS.md changes.

items.title: Environment-Aware Orchestration
items.text:
The portable orchestration skills prefer instructions from the target project before their bundled defaults. When a project provides its own local role catalog, those project-local roles remain authoritative; otherwise Claude Code uses the oh-my-claudecode catalog.

The execution shape intentionally differs by agent:

  • Claude Code prefers user- or project-owned routing when available. The published adapters/ templates offer a genericized starting point that selects roles by capability; they do not pin model versions or encode one user's routing policy, and a private overlay or project file always wins.
  • Codex defaults to a compact plan -> executor -> validation flow and adds research or review roles only for distinct risks.

The workflow remains shared; only delegation mechanics and tool-specific configuration belong in an adapter or target project.

items.title: Project-Specific Rules
items.text:
Keep stack- and domain-specific instructions in the target project, for example:

  • AGENTS.md for Codex or other compatible agents
  • CLAUDE.md for Claude Code
  • .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md or .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md for truly project-local skills

Do not copy shared skills into multiple tracked directories in this repository, and do not duplicate a skill body into an adapter.

items.title: Releases and dependency updates
items.text: This repository uses Release Please for versioning and changelog generation, and Renovate for pinned GitHub Actions updates. The workflows rendered by the quokkify/ci-kit Copier template are the exception: the toolkit owns the versions inside them and delivers them through copier update.

items.title: Release flow
items.text:
1. Open pull requests with a Conventional Commit title. The scope is optional:
type(optional-scope): short summary
  1. Merge the pull request into main. The squash commit title must remain conventional.
  2. Release Please updates or opens a release pull request containing the next version and CHANGELOG.md entries.
  3. Merge the release pull request after its checks pass.
  4. Release Please creates the organization-standard vX.Y.Z Git tag and GitHub release.

The manifest records the latest released version. The bootstrap-sha marks the 0.7.1 release commit as the migration boundary from historical skills-vX.Y.Z tags to the organization-standard vX.Y.Z format, without retagging past releases. The simple release type is used because this repository has no package manifest.

Release impact follows Conventional Commits:

  • fix(scope): ... and perf(scope): ... produce a patch release;
  • feat(scope): ... produces a minor release;
  • a breaking change marked with ! produces a major release;
  • docs, ci, build, refactor, test, and chore do not create a release by themselves.

The PR Title workflow enforces the title format before merge. When squash merging, verify the final commit title in GitHub because Release Please reads merged commit history rather than the pull request body.

items.title: Renovate flow
items.text:
.github/renovate.json was generated from the Copier answers and is owned by this repository from then on; the template does not rewrite it. It extends the shared public base and GitHub Actions presets, which is how toolkit-owned Renovate policy reaches this repository. Renovate keeps immutable action SHAs current while preserving readable version comments.

Renovate is disabled for the workflow paths the template owns, including .github/workflows/release.yml. Without that exclusion the same pin has two owners: Renovate moves it, the next copier update lands on the moved pin, and the update conflicts in a file this repository never edited. Versions inside those files change only when the template is updated.

The Renovate Config workflow runs:

  • when .github/renovate.json or its validation workflow changes;
  • weekly, to detect incompatibility with newer Renovate versions;
  • manually through workflow_dispatch.

It executes renovate-config-validator --strict .github/renovate.json. Renovate pull requests must pass the normal repository checks before merge. Major dependency updates still require explicit review; do not bypass branch protection or security review for an automated update.

items.title: Toolkit references
items.text:
Every workflow that calls quokkify/ci-kit references it at the version recorded as toolkit_version in .copier-answers.release.yml, in one of two accepted forms:

  • the exact release tag, for example @v3.2.1 — what the template renders, and what every consumer that calls the toolkit's release workflow uses;
  • a full 40-character commit digest carrying that tag as a comment, for example @7bc13e13… # v3.2.1.

The template-owned check in .github/workflows/validate.yml enforces this across every workflow, and tests/test_release_configuration.py asserts it for the release caller. A tag is mutable and a digest is not, so the digest form remains available for a deliberate, hand-maintained pin. It is not the default here: ADR-0002 records why this repository references the toolkit by tag and what that trades away.

items.title: Reviewing and Promoting Skills
items.text: The skill-review workflow turns reusable lessons into reviewable skill changes without publishing local agent state automatically.

items.title: When to use it
items.text: Use the workflow after significant work when a procedure, correction, workaround, or missing instruction would help with future tasks. Skip routine operations, temporary progress, one-off facts, and project-specific rules.

items.title: Promotion flow
items.text:
significant task
    -> classify the lesson
    -> search existing skills
    -> private candidate
    -> privacy and portability audit
    -> task approval or durable repository opt-in
    -> branch or worktree
    -> validation and secret scan
    -> pull request
    -> normal review and merge

A candidate is not a published skill. Keep it outside the shared repository until promotion is approved or an applicable durable draft-queue opt-in is verified.

items.title: Optional rolling draft queue
items.text:
A repository owner may pre-authorize completed, public-safe improvements to accumulate in a rolling draft pull request. Configure one automation/skill-improvements/<lane> branch per device or independently running agent and use skill-promotion-queue as the completion workflow.

This opt-in replaces repeated publication prompts only. It does not authorize direct pushes to the default branch, force-push, automatic merge, or publication of private runtime state. The agent must still perform the privacy and portability audit, deterministic validation, and configured secret scanning. Independent review may be deferred until the owner handles the batch.

items.title: Decisions
items.text:
Every review ends with one of three decisions:

  • patch-existing: an existing skill already owns the workflow;
  • create-new: the workflow is reusable and has no suitable owner;
  • no-change: the lesson is duplicated, private, temporary, or too narrow.

Prefer patching an existing broad skill over creating a one-incident micro-skill.

items.title: Public boundary
items.text:
Before promotion:

  1. Remove credentials, identities, private paths, internal URLs, infrastructure details, client context, and raw transcripts.
  2. Replace real values with fictional placeholders.
  3. Confirm that the procedure remains useful outside the task that produced it.
  4. Review the complete diff and untracked files.
  5. Run ./scripts/validate.sh --full; it performs repository validation, builds the documentation, and scans the full Git history with Gitleaks.

See the repository SECURITY.md for the complete public-content policy.

items.title: Claude Code and Codex
items.text: Install the repository skills normally. In Claude Code, invoke the installed skill-review skill when significant work produces a reusable lesson; the shared global instruction base (adapters/shared/AGENTS.base.md, installed by scripts/bootstrap.sh) carries a "Skill Library Self-Improvement" section that prompts this review. The optional Codex AGENTS.md adapter adds a post-task review prompt as well. By default, promotion requires task-specific approval before a branch or pull request is created. A durable repository-scoped opt-in may instead route eligible changes through skill-promotion-queue.

items.title: Hermes
items.text:
Hermes can discover this repository through skills.external_dirs:

skills:
  external_dirs:
    - /absolute/path/to/skills/skills

Point the setting at the canonical skills/ directory. Restart Hermes or begin a new session after changing skill discovery settings.

External directories are not read-only. If the Hermes process can write to the checkout, skill-management tools can modify it. Treat the checkout as a shared Git source: inspect skills with skills_list and skill_view, but make approved updates in an isolated branch or worktree rather than patching the external directory in place.

If a local Hermes skill and an external skill have the same name, the local skill takes precedence. Resolve that conflict before assuming the shared version is active.

items.title: Candidate format
items.text:
The bundled skills/skill-management/skill-review/templates/candidate.md template records:

  • the reusable trigger;
  • the target skill or proposed name;
  • generalized evidence;
  • the proposed change;
  • pitfalls and verification;
  • privacy and portability checks;
  • the promotion plan and approval state.

Do not commit a filled candidate merely to preserve task history. Only the approved, generalized skill change belongs in the public repository.

items.title: renovate-adoption-review Implementation Plan
items.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: Ship a portable hub skill that turns a Renovate update (open PR or a batch of merged ones) into grounded, cited adoption changes in the consumer repository.

Architecture: A deterministic POSIX sh CLI (renovate_adoption.sh) fetches data through gh and pipes it into a jq module (renovate_adoption.jq) that parses Renovate PR bodies, classifies update types, applies triage and aggregates retro intervals. SKILL.md plus references/ drive the model-side work (sources, grounding, edits, child PR, issue). Python unittest tests run the CLI against recorded fixtures through a stub gh on PATH.

Tech Stack: POSIX sh, jq ≥ 1.6, GitHub CLI gh, Python 3 unittest (hub convention), hub scripts/validate.sh.

Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-07-renovate-adoption-review-design.md

items.title: Global Constraints
items.text:
• Skill directory: skills/repository/renovate-adoption-review/; frontmatter name: renovate-adoption-review, single-line description ≤ 1024 chars.
  • Helper is POSIX sh (#!/bin/sh, no bashisms), depends only on gh and jq.
  • Exit codes: 0 success, 2 usage error, 3 gh/network/missing-tool failure with a message on stderr; never print an empty result on failure.
  • Allowlist file in the consumer: .github/renovate-adoption.json, shape {"allow": ["<package>", ...]}; absent file = empty list.
  • Child branch prefix adopt/; marker <!-- adoption-base: <sha> -->; finding touching more than 10 files is proposed, not applied.
  • Public repo: no machine paths, employer data, tokens; fixtures are sanitized copies of public quokkify PRs.
  • Tests run via python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v; full gate ./scripts/validate.sh --full.

items.title: Review Focus
items.text:
• Grouped Renovate PR (several table rows, mixed types): verdict must be candidate if any row qualifies, with every row listed.
  • Docker-style versions (21-jdk-alpine → 25-jdk-alpine, 3.12-slim): classify by leading numeric components, ignore the suffix.
  • 0.x versions: a minor bump 0.4 → 0.5 is a major (semver convention).
  • PR body without the updates table (manual edits, lock-file maintenance): no crash; skip with reason.
  • retro --since given a tag or SHA, not a date: resolved to that commit's date via git log -1 --format=%cI.

Each line has a test in the task that owns the code (Tasks 1 and 2).

  • Step 4: Implement the jq module. parse_updates: take table rows between the header line starting | Package | and the first blank line; package = link text of column 1, sourceUrl = its href with host redirect.github.com → github.com; from/to = the two backticked values in column 2 split on →. releaseNotesUrls = unique https://(redirect.)?github.com/<o>/<r>/(releases/tag|compare)/... links anywhere in the body, normalized. strip leading "v"; if both match ^[0-9a-f]{7,40}$ → digest
take leading numeric components (split on [.-], stop at first non-numeric)
if from has fewer components and to starts with from's components → pin
no numeric prefix on either side → unknown
first differing index: 0 → major; 1 → (from[0]==0 ? major : minor); else patch

items.title: discussion-card Implementation Plan
items.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: A hub skill that turns one Markdown file plus an agent-written card.yaml into one offline, interactive HTML discussion card. Mermaid flowcharts become clickable diagrams, and the build is gated by checks.

Architecture: - discuss.sh builds and reuses a pinned venv and a sha256-verified Mermaid cache. - It runs plan.py (validate), build.py (page model and HTML), mermaid_svg.py (Mermaid rendered in headless Chrome into static SVG) and check.py (gates). - A generic engine.js/engine.css provides all interactivity and reads only #card-config and data-spot elements.

Tech Stack: Python ≥3.10 (unittest, markdown-it-py set, PyYAML), POSIX sh, headless Chrome, @mermaid-js/tiny 12.3.0 (MIT), vanilla JS/CSS, Playwright 1.65.0 with node --test for browser tests.

Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-09-discussion-card-design.md

items.title: Global Constraints
items.text:
• Skill dir: skills/software-development/discussion-card/. No runtime imports from md-to-html-page. Copied files keep a provenance line in SKILL.md.
  • Python ≥3.10. Scripts run as python -I. Third-party Python only from the pinned scripts/requirements.txt: markdown-it-py==4.2.0, mdit-py-plugins==0.6.1, linkify-it-py==2.2.0, mdurl==0.1.2, Pygments==2.21.0, PyYAML==6.0.3.
  • Cache root ${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/discussion-card/. Venv dir <root>/<sha256(requirements)[:12]> with marker .discussion-card. DISCUSS_VENV overrides it; the script refuses to replace an existing dir without the marker (exit 3).
  • scripts/mermaid.lock:
  • version=12.3.0
  • url=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@mermaid-js/tiny@12.3.0/dist/mermaid.tiny.js
  • sha256=c41f5236091b83f524c4940f97a16b2b14a76f21ff84aea4fd6b66421d8a2a9a
  • Cached as <root>/mermaid-12.3.0.js; DISCUSS_MERMAID overrides the path. A sha mismatch is exit 3.
  • Chrome: CHROME_BIN, else /Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome, else google-chrome/chromium on PATH. Flags: --headless=new --disable-gpu --allow-file-access-from-files --virtual-time-budget=15000 --dump-dom.
  • Mermaid: securityLevel: 'strict', themeVariables.fontSize: '16px'. Rendered node DOM id is <renderId>-flowchart-<nodeId>-<n> (verified on 12.3.0).
  • Spot ids:
  • Mermaid node: <chapter-slug>-<nodeId>.
  • Other spots: <chapter-slug>-<kind>-<sha1(normalised text)[:6]>, with collisions suffixed -2, -3 in source order.
  • kind ∈ p|li|tr|callout|code|intro|q.
  • Chapter slug: ASCII, transliterated, lowercase, hyphenated, ≤40 chars.
  • Normalised text means whitespace collapsed and stripped.
  • Storage key discussion-card:<slug>:v1. Presenter mode key <storage key>:mode. State shape exactly as in spec §Engine.
  • Check line: PASS words=<n> extra=<n> spots=<n> diagrams=<n>|runtime offline=ok [ids=kept|ids=-k], or FAIL <gate>: <reason> followed by up to 5 sample lines.
  • Exit codes: 0 pass; 1 check fail or build error (no output written); 2 bad args or plan schema; 3 environment.
  • Output <name>.card.html next to the source unless -o. An existing output is moved to <name>.card.backup.html before replacing.
  • Diagram text ≥14px at scale 1. Diagram SVGs are never scaled down.
  • No network at view time. No innerHTML with source or user data in engine.js.
  • Skill files contain no machine paths (/Users/, /home/) and no e-mails except example.com. These are checked by the hub test.
  • UI labels in ru and en; --ui auto picks ru when Cyrillic letters are the majority.

1. A source with no H2 and no Mermaid builds one chapter, with no diagram gates applied and no crash. Pinned in Task 4: test_no_h2_single_chapter.

  5. An imported JSON with junk, foreign ids or huge strings is sanitised: unknown statuses are dropped and strings capped (comment 4000, names 80/500). Pinned in Task 8: import sanitises junk.

items.title: md-to-html-page Implementation Plan
items.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: A hub skill that renders one Markdown file into one self-contained, offline, genre-aware .html page and refuses to emit it unless an independent fidelity and offline gate passes.

Architecture: mdpage.sh owns the venv and the render → check → atomic-move pipeline. render.py turns markdown-it-py tokens into a page with component transforms and inlined assets; check.py re-derives the reference text with a plain CommonMark parser and compares it to the rendered HTML; mermaid_view.py builds a derived text view of flowcharts.

Tech Stack: Python ≥ 3.10, POSIX sh, markdown-it-py, mdit-py-plugins, linkify-it-py, mdurl, Pygments; stdlib unittest and html.parser.

Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-09-md-to-html-page-design.md

items.title: Global Constraints
items.text:
• Skill directory: skills/software-development/md-to-html-page/; frontmatter name: md-to-html-page (must equal the directory name).
  • Pins in scripts/requirements.txt, exactly: markdown-it-py==4.2.0, mdit-py-plugins==0.6.1, linkify-it-py==2.2.0, mdurl==0.1.2, Pygments==2.21.0.
  • Venv path: ${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/md-to-html-page/<first 12 hex of sha256(requirements.txt)>; every Python call uses -I.
  • Output: no <script src>, no remote <link>/<img>/<iframe>/<object>, no @import, no url(http, no web fonts; CSP meta exactly default-src 'none'; img-src data:; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'unsafe-inline'.
  • Deterministic: no timestamps, random values, absolute paths, or dict-order-dependent output.
  • Added non-source text carries data-chrome; source-derived views carry data-derived.
  • Front matter never appears in the page; only type: and title: are read.
  • Exit codes: 0 pass, 1 render error or check FAIL, 2 bad arguments, 3 venv setup failure.
  • Public-safe: fixtures and tests are synthetic; no employer, project, or person names, no machine paths, no real e-mail addresses. Company-name grep is a manual pre-PR step and the name list is never committed.
  • Shell scripts are POSIX sh (no bashisms, no GNU-only flags).
  • Hub tests run through python3 -m unittest discover -s tests (see scripts/validate.sh).
  • Dev interpreter $V: for Tasks 1–4, V="${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/md-to-html-page/dev"; from Task 5 on, V="$(dirname "$(skills/software-development/md-to-html-page/scripts/mdpage.sh --python)")/..". All skill tests use stdlib unittest.

Spec amendment (do in Task 1): the spec says check.py is "stdlib only". The order gate needs a Markdown parser to strip markup, so check.py uses markdown-it-py in plain commonmark mode with only table and strikethrough enabled and none of the renderer's plugins or rules. It still shares no code with render.py. Edit that spec line accordingly.

items.title: mr-glab-review Implementation Plan
items.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: A public, organisation-neutral skill mr-glab-review that reviews a GitLab MR with the human reviewer item by item, stages approved comments as draft notes in a light, formatted style, and publishes them in one batch.

Architecture: One skill directory in the hub (skills/repository/mr-glab-review/): a phased SKILL.md, two reference files (GitLab API recipes, comment style), and one stdlib-only Python helper for the fragile parts (MR URL parsing, diff-line mapping, draft-note payloads). A private wrapper skill living outside the hub passes an organisation profile; it is out of scope for hub commits and handled in the last task.

Tech Stack: Markdown skill files; Python ≥3.10 stdlib only (argparse, json, re, dataclasses, urllib.parse); unittest; glab api at runtime.

Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-10-mr-glab-review-design.md

items.title: Global Constraints
items.text:
• Skill path: skills/repository/mr-glab-review/SKILL.md; frontmatter name: mr-glab-review; single-line description ≤ 1024 chars.
  • Public boundary: no employer names, hosts, trackers, ticket keys, project IDs, people, machine paths (/Users/, /home/) or real e-mails (only example.com). Examples use invented names (OrderGenerator, UserSteps, example.gitlab.com, project group/app).
  • No new dependencies (pyproject.toml dependencies = [] stays empty).
  • All runtime API calls via glab api; project ID and diff_refs resolved from the MR, never hardcoded.
  • Nothing visible to the MR author before Phase 4 and an explicit yes; inline comments only on lines present in the diff.
  • Comment checklist: first line stands alone; ≤ ~120 words excluding code and <details>; concrete suggestion present; no "wrong"/"bug" without evidence; language per profile (default: MR description language).
  • Markers: 🔍/🙂 double-check · 🧹 cleanup · ✂️ simplify · 🔀 mismatch · 💡 idea/non-blocker · 🔄 process.
  • ./scripts/validate.sh --full passes before any push.

items.title: Review Focus
items.text:
• A comment targeting a line outside any hunk (e.g. a constant declared far from changed lines) → helper reports "not in diff" and the skill falls back to a general note naming file:line. Test in Task 1 (test_line_outside_hunks_is_not_in_diff).
  • A deleted line or a line in a renamed file → mapping uses the new path and never returns a number for removed lines. Tests in Task 1 (test_removed_line_has_no_new_number, test_renamed_file_uses_new_path).
  • Duplicate line text in one file (e.g. two identical .build();) → mapping by text must refuse to guess and return all candidates. Test in Task 1 (test_ambiguous_text_returns_all_candidates).
  • Self-hosted GitLab under a sub-path or with nested groups (https://host/a/b/c/-/merge_requests/7) → URL parser keeps the full project path. Test in Task 1 (test_nested_group_url).
  • Reviewer interrupts mid-loop → existing drafts on the MR are detected in Phase 0 and the loop resumes from the state file instead of duplicating comments. Pinned by the SKILL.md resume section and exercised in Task 4 scenario 3.
